newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan's stock warning sends investors to gold shelter.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan's stock warning sends investors to gold shelter.

text.p: Gold traders were popping champagne corks as investors rushed back into the market this week, boosting gold prices and gold mining shares, thanks to Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's bluntest warning yet over the stock market's lofty levels.
Greenspan again showed his knack for getting Wall Street's attention, as his latest comments, which suggested that the raging bull market was foaming at the mouth, roiled stocks.
But the Fed chief unwittingly became one of the world's best gold market promoters.

"Greenspan may not be directly promoting gold but effectively, he has now joined the choir of gold traders, by scaring people away from the stock market," said John Geraghty at North American Equity Services, a consulting firm.

In his semi-annual economic testimony to Congress, Greenspan conceded that the economic outlook was good but argued that Wall Street investors may have thrown caution to the wind in bidding up prices.

"Such caution seems especially warranted with regard to the sharp rise in equity prices during the past two years," he told the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday. "These gains have obviously raised questions of sustainability."
Greenspan's words were more blunt than in December when his remarks about the irrational exuberance of financial markets also touched off a stock selloff.
This time, he warned that speculative bubbles always burst, underscoring the threat that a stock market collapse could be the source of economic instability.
"Greenspan unintentionally told people that gold may be a better place to be than stocks, which seem to be saturated with the hoard of cash," Geraghty said.
Gold has been in the dog house for years but the precious metal now appears to have regained some respectability.
After collapsing to a low of nearly four years at $336.15 an ounce on Feb. 12, gold this week climbed $29 to $365.00.

Stocks headed in the other direction. The blue-chip Dow Jones industrial average was sent skidding three days in a row. On Friday, the index closed 47.33 points lower at 6,877.74, and for the week, it was down 53.88 points.
In December, the stock market had a shorter attention span as Greenspan's market warning set off a one-day selloff and stocks later rallied strongly.

"Greenspan's statements this week were more blunt and stronger," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer for First Albany Corp. "He fired a cross across the bow in December and he fired another shot this week but that shot was a larger missile and it came much closer to the ship."
It may be time for the stock market bulls to call time out.

"The market has gotten to levels at which stocks were overvalued and that it is time for cautious and price sensitive investors to take it easy for a while," Johnson said. "My guess is that investors will take Greenspan's advice and if stocks go down, perhaps gold will turn into an alternative."

Greenspan has never been counted among gold's cheerleaders. In fact, the central bank chief has preached the sermon about the gold-inflation link -- the economic theory that a rising price of gold is a precursor to future inflationary pressures.

But some critics believe that the link is nonsense. Gold reflects inflation, they say, and it does not cause commodity prices to go up, just as the Dow Jones index cannot be blamed for the current surge in stocks.

Gold mining stocks have traditionally been viewed by Wall Street as a hedge against inflation, but in the absence of notable inflation pressures, investors are turning to the shares for another reason. They are buying the gold stocks as shelter -- a place to hide in the event the stock market bubble bursts.
This protection against the vagaries of the high-flying market has buoyed gold shares, as the ranks of Nervous Nellies have grown.

According to Lipper Analytical Services, a firm that tracks mutual funds, the value of gold-oriented mutual funds has risen nearly 3 percent in the first two months of this year, while at the same period, the Dow Jones index has gone up 7 percent. Last year, gold mutual funds racked up a total gain of less than 8 percent.

"Investors are looking across the valley and they are valuing the shares of gold companies based on their future earnings and the gold reserves of individual producers," said James Turk, strategic advisor for Midas Fund, precious metals mutual.
"From a long-term perspective, there are also a lot of reasons to be acccumulating gold bullion at these low levels, which are the lowest since the early 1970s when adjusted for inflation." he said.
James Dines, publisher of the Dines Letter in Belvedere, Calif., believes that "we are about to embark on a very lucrative" precious metals rally.
"The whole inflation hedge sector is up across the board -- gold, diamonds, copper," he said.

"Everyone has gone for this hook line and sinker dogma that there is no inflation, and it can't go up and there's no possibility of inflation rising...and that's not what the precious metals market is saying," Dines said.
Indeed, commodity prices have been going since the start of the year.

The price of nickel, mainly used in making stainless steel, jumped this week to the highest level since last May and copper was at an 8-1/2-month high, while palladium soared to levels unseen since August 1995. Aluminum also bustled higher.
Grain prices are the highest in about four months and coffee has soared nearly 50 percent in the first six weeks of the year.
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite index fell 3.66 points to 1,309.00, down 25.32 on the week.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks lost 4.25 points to 790.82, a drop of 10.95 from last Friday. The American Stock Exchange index was off 0.93 at 594.24, down 3.05 on the week.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks fell 2.38 to 415.51, down 5.50 from last Friday.
